question: How does 3D Gaussian Splatting render a novel view?
ground_truth: 3DGS rasterizes the scene's 3D Gaussians by projecting them to 2D and alpha-blending them, using an image formation model equivalent to NeRF's. A tile-based renderer splits the screen into 16x16 tiles, culls Gaussians against the view frustum and each tile, and duplicates each Gaussian for every tile it overlaps with a key combining view-space depth and tile ID. All instances are sorted with a single GPU radix sort; each tile then accumulates color and alpha by traversing its sorted list front to back, stopping a pixel once alpha saturates. This gives real-time (>=30 fps) rendering at 1080p.

question: What is the multiresolution hash encoding in Instant-NGP and why does it work?
ground_truth: Instant-NGP augments a small neural network with a multiresolution hierarchy of hash tables holding trainable feature vectors. A cascade of grids is mapped to fixed-size arrays; at fine resolutions the array is indexed with a spatial hash, so several grid points can collide in one entry. Colliding gradients average, so the largest gradients (the most important fine detail) dominate, and the multiresolution structure lets the network disambiguate collisions. The small network reduces floating-point and memory operations, giving speedups of several orders of magnitude: training in seconds and rendering in tens of milliseconds at 1920x1080.

question: How does Mip-NeRF reduce aliasing compared to NeRF?
ground_truth: Mip-NeRF casts a cone from each pixel instead of a single ray, and renders conical frustums approximated by Gaussians rather than infinitesimal points. Each Gaussian region is featurized with an integrated positional encoding (IPE), which encodes a 3D position together with its surrounding volume, producing prefiltered, scale-aware features. This reduces aliasing artifacts and improves fine detail, while being about 7% faster than NeRF and half the size.

question: How does Mip-NeRF 360 handle unbounded scenes?
ground_truth: Mip-NeRF 360 extends mip-NeRF with three components: a non-linear scene parameterization that allocates more capacity to nearby content and less to distant content; online distillation, in which a small proposal MLP predicts density (not color) to resample intervals for a large NeRF MLP and is supervised by the NeRF MLP's histogram weights rather than the images; and a distortion-based regularizer. It reduces mean-squared error by 57% compared to mip-NeRF on unbounded 360-degree scenes.

question: How does NeuS turn a signed distance function into volume rendering weights?
ground_truth: NeuS represents the surface as the zero-level set of an SDF and introduces an S-density, phi_s(f(x)), a logistic density distribution applied to the signed distance. It then derives a weight function w(t) along each ray from the SDF and states requirements for it, designing a rendering scheme that is unbiased in the first-order approximation of the SDF, so that surfaces, including thin structures and self-occluded objects, can be learned accurately from 2D images without foreground masks.

question: What does Plenoxels use instead of a neural network, and how fast is it?
ground_truth: Plenoxels represent the scene as a sparse 3D voxel grid in which each voxel stores opacity and spherical harmonic coefficients, with no neural network. The grid is optimized end-to-end from calibrated photos with a differentiable rendering loss plus a total variation regularizer. Optimization takes about 11 minutes on bounded scenes versus roughly a day for NeRF, and 27 minutes on unbounded scenes versus roughly 4 days for NeRF++, more than a 100x speedup.

question: How does TensoRF factorize a radiance field?
ground_truth: TensoRF models the radiance field as a 4D scene tensor and factorizes it into compact low-rank components. CP decomposition factorizes it into rank-one components with compact vectors, giving fast reconstruction (under 30 minutes) with a model under 4 MB. The new vector-matrix (VM) decomposition relaxes the low-rank constraint for two modes, factorizing into vector and matrix factors; it improves quality further, reconstructs in under 10 minutes, and stays under 75 MB.

question: How does DUSt3R reconstruct a scene without camera calibration or poses?
ground_truth: DUSt3R casts pairwise reconstruction as regression of pointmaps, relaxing the constraints of projective camera models, and works without any prior camera calibration or viewpoint poses. Pointmaps encode scene geometry, the pixel-to-scene-point relation, and the relation between the two viewpoints. The network uses standard Transformer encoders and decoders so it can leverage pretrained models. For more than two images, a global alignment step expresses all pairwise pointmaps in a common reference frame.

question: Why does BARF use coarse-to-fine positional encoding when optimizing camera poses?
ground_truth: BARF (Bundle-Adjusting NeRF) jointly optimizes a NeRF and imperfect or unknown camera poses. It shows that naively applying positional encoding hurts registration: the encoding lets NeRF fit high-frequency functions but makes it more susceptible to suboptimal registration. Drawing on a theoretical connection to classical image alignment, BARF applies coarse-to-fine registration, gradually enabling higher-frequency components of the positional encoding during optimization.

question: How does SplaTAM track the camera using Gaussians?
ground_truth: SplaTAM is an online tracking-and-mapping system built on a 3D Gaussian map for RGB-D SLAM. It renders a silhouette mask, the accumulated opacity of the Gaussian map for a view, to identify which parts of the scene are already mapped, and uses only those parts when optimizing the camera pose. For speed it removes view-dependent appearance and uses isotropic (spherical) Gaussians. It reports up to 2x better camera pose estimation, map construction, and novel-view synthesis than prior methods.

question: How does Mip-Splatting fix aliasing artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting?
ground_truth: 3DGS shows strong artifacts when the sampling rate changes (focal length or camera distance), which Mip-Splatting attributes to the lack of 3D frequency constraints and the use of a 2D screen-space dilation filter. It adds a 3D smoothing filter that limits the size of 3D Gaussians based on the maximal sampling frequency induced by the training views, removing high-frequency artifacts when zooming in, and replaces 2D dilation with a 2D Mip filter that simulates a 2D box filter, mitigating aliasing and dilation problems.

question: How does 2D Gaussian Splatting differ from 3D Gaussian Splatting?
ground_truth: 2DGS collapses the 3D volume into a set of 2D oriented planar Gaussian disks (surfel-like primitives) instead of 3D Gaussian ellipsoids. These provide view-consistent geometry and model surfaces intrinsically. It uses a perspective-correct 2D splatting process based on ray-splat intersection and rasterization, and adds depth distortion and normal consistency terms, yielding geometrically accurate surface reconstruction.

question: How does NeRF in the Wild handle photos with varying lighting and transient objects?
ground_truth: NeRF-W models per-image appearance variation (exposure, lighting, weather, post-processing) with an appearance embedding optimized per image in a learned low-dimensional latent space, following Generative Latent Optimization. It also models the scene as shared static content plus image-dependent transient content, using a secondary transient radiance field combined with a data-dependent uncertainty field that captures observation noise and reduces the influence of transient occluders on the static scene.

question: How does pixelNeRF synthesize novel views from one or a few images?
ground_truth: pixelNeRF conditions a NeRF on input images in a fully convolutional manner, predicting a continuous neural scene representation from one or a few images. Training across many scenes lets it learn a scene prior, so it performs novel view synthesis feed-forward from as few as one view, without per-scene optimization. It is evaluated on ShapeNet single-image view synthesis, including held-out objects and unseen categories.

question: What does VGGT predict from a set of images?
ground_truth: VGGT (Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer) is a feed-forward network that directly infers the key 3D attributes of a scene, namely camera parameters, point maps, depth maps, and 3D point tracks, from one, a few, or hundreds of views. It reconstructs in under one second and still outperforms methods that need post-processing with geometry optimization. Its pretrained features also improve downstream non-rigid point tracking and feed-forward novel view synthesis.

question: How does Zip-NeRF combine grid-based NeRFs with anti-aliasing?
ground_truth: Grid-based models like Instant-NGP train fast but lack an explicit notion of scale and alias, while mip-NeRF 360's cone-based anti-aliasing is not natively compatible with grids. Zip-NeRF integrates iNGP's pyramid of grids into mip-NeRF 360 by turning each conical frustum into a set of isotropic Gaussians through multisampling and feature downweighting. It reports error rates 8%-77% lower than either prior technique and trains 24x faster than mip-NeRF 360.

question: How does 3D Gaussian Splatting as MCMC replace the adaptive density control heuristics?
ground_truth: It treats the set of 3D Gaussians as Markov Chain Monte Carlo samples from an underlying distribution describing the scene. Adding noise turns the Gaussian updates into Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics updates, and densification and pruning are rewritten as a deterministic state transition of MCMC samples, with cloning replaced by a relocalization scheme that approximately preserves sample probability. This removes the hand-tuned cloning and splitting heuristics of 3DGS, which need many hyperparameters and can fail on some scenes.

question: How does D-NeRF model a dynamic scene over time?
ground_truth: D-NeRF adds time as an extra input and splits learning into two stages: a deformation network learns a mapping (x, y, z, t) -> (dx, dy, dz) from each point at time t to a canonical scene configuration, and a canonical network encodes the scene in that canonical space. After training it can render novel images while controlling both camera view and time.

question: Compare how NeRF, Instant-NGP and 3D Gaussian Splatting trade off training speed and quality.
ground_truth: NeRF represents the scene with a single MLP mapping 5D coordinates to density and color, using positional encoding and hierarchical sampling; quality is high but training is slow (Plenoxels reports roughly a day per scene for NeRF). Instant-NGP keeps a neural field but replaces most of the network with a multiresolution hash encoding and a tiny MLP, training in seconds to minutes. 3DGS drops the neural field for explicit 3D Gaussians with a tile-based rasterizer: it matches InstantNGP and Plenoxels quality after 5-10 minutes, reaches quality on par with Mip-NeRF360 after 35-45 minutes (versus 48 hours), and renders in real time (>=30 fps at 1080p), whereas the other fast methods cannot reach state-of-the-art quality with more training.

question: Compare how NeuS and VolSDF convert a signed distance function into volume density.
ground_truth: Both represent geometry as an SDF and render it with volume rendering. NeuS defines an S-density using a logistic density applied to the SDF and derives a weight function along the ray designed to be unbiased in the first-order approximation of the SDF. VolSDF defines the volume density as the Laplace cumulative distribution function applied to the SDF; this gives an inductive bias on geometry, a bound on the opacity approximation error that enables accurate ray sampling, and efficient disentanglement of shape and appearance.

question: How does NICE-SLAM's scene representation differ from iMAP's?
ground_truth: iMAP showed that a single MLP can be the only scene representation in a real-time RGB-D SLAM system, trained live with keyframes and information-guided pixel sampling (tracking at 10 Hz, mapping at 2 Hz). Its key limitation is that one MLP represents the entire scene and can only be updated globally with each new, possibly partial observation. NICE-SLAM instead uses a hierarchical, multi-level scene representation that incorporates local information and is optimized with pre-trained geometric priors, enabling detailed reconstruction of large indoor scenes.

question: How do pixelSplat and MVSplat predict 3D Gaussians from sparse views, and how do they compare?
ground_truth: pixelSplat regresses Gaussian parameters for two-view reconstruction. It uses a multi-view epipolar transformer to infer the per-scene scale factor and, to avoid local minima, predicts a dense probability distribution over 3D from which Gaussian means are sampled, made differentiable with a reparameterization trick. MVSplat instead localizes Gaussian centers with a plane-sweep cost volume whose cross-view feature similarities give geometry cues for depth. Compared with pixelSplat, MVSplat uses 10x fewer parameters, infers more than 2x faster, and gives higher appearance and geometry quality with better cross-dataset generalization.

question: How do SplaTAM and Gaussian Splatting SLAM differ in their sensor setup and tracking approach?
ground_truth: SplaTAM targets RGB-D SLAM: it renders a silhouette mask of accumulated opacity to restrict pose optimization to mapped regions, and uses isotropic Gaussians without view-dependent appearance for speed. Gaussian Splatting SLAM (Matsuki et al.) presents 3DGS for monocular SLAM, the hardest setup, extendable to RGB-D when depth is available; it formulates camera tracking as direct optimization against the 3D Gaussians, giving fast, robust tracking with a wide basin of convergence, removing the need for offline SfM poses.

question: Summarize how anti-aliasing has been addressed in radiance fields and Gaussian splatting.
ground_truth: Mip-NeRF replaces rays with cones and featurizes conical frustums with an integrated positional encoding, giving prefiltered scale-aware features. Mip-NeRF 360 keeps this cone-based reasoning and extends it to unbounded scenes. Zip-NeRF brings anti-aliasing to fast grid-based models by converting each frustum into isotropic Gaussians via multisampling and feature downweighting, combining mip-NeRF 360 with Instant-NGP grids. For 3D Gaussian Splatting, Mip-Splatting attributes zoom artifacts to missing 3D frequency constraints and 2D dilation, and adds a 3D smoothing filter plus a 2D Mip filter.

question: Summarize how camera poses are recovered or avoided in pose-free neural reconstruction.
ground_truth: BARF jointly optimizes NeRF and camera poses using coarse-to-fine positional encoding, motivated by classical image alignment. DUSt3R avoids explicit calibration by regressing pointmaps from uncalibrated, unposed image pairs and globally aligning them for more views. VGGT goes further with a feed-forward transformer that directly predicts camera parameters, depth maps, point maps, and tracks from one to hundreds of views in under a second.
